learningObjectives.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions and energy transfer to/from the surroundings
Reaction pathway diagrams and activation energy
Enthalpy change (ΔH) and its sign convention
Bond breaking, bond making and bond energy calculations

questions.q: What happens to the temperature of the surroundings during an exothermic reaction?
questions.explain: An exothermic reaction transfers thermal energy to the surroundings, raising their temperature.

questions.q: What happens to the temperature of the surroundings during an endothermic reaction?
questions.explain: An endothermic reaction takes in thermal energy from the surroundings, lowering their temperature.

questions.q: What is the sign of the enthalpy change, ΔH, for an exothermic reaction?
questions.explain: ΔH is negative for exothermic reactions because thermal energy is given out to the surroundings.

questions.q: What is the sign of the enthalpy change, ΔH, for an endothermic reaction?
questions.explain: ΔH is positive for endothermic reactions because thermal energy is taken in from the surroundings.

questions.q: What is the activation energy, Ea, of a reaction?
options: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have to react
The total energy released when bonds form
The energy stored in the products
The average energy of all the particles
questions.explain: Activation energy is defined as the minimum energy that colliding particles must have in order to react.

questions.q: Is the breaking of chemical bonds exothermic or endothermic?
questions.explain: Breaking bonds requires energy to be taken in, so it is an endothermic process.

questions.q: Is the making (forming) of chemical bonds exothermic or endothermic?
questions.explain: Forming bonds releases energy, so bond making is an exothermic process.

questions.q: What name is given to the transfer of thermal energy during a chemical reaction?
questions.explain: The transfer of thermal energy during a reaction is called the enthalpy change, ΔH.

questions.q: On a reaction pathway diagram for an exothermic reaction, how do the energy levels of the products compare with the reactants?
options: The products are at a lower energy level than the reactants
The products are at a higher energy level than the reactants
The products and reactants are at the same energy level
The products have no defined energy level
questions.explain: In an exothermic reaction energy is released, so the products lie below the reactants on the pathway diagram.

questions.q: Which of the following reactions is exothermic?
options: The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
questions.explain: Combustion releases thermal energy to the surroundings, making it exothermic.

questions.q: Which of the following is an endothermic process?
options: The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
The neutralisation of an acid by an alkali
The reaction of magnesium with dilute acid
questions.explain: Thermal decomposition takes in thermal energy to break the compound down, so it is endothermic.

questions.q: Why is breaking a chemical bond an endothermic process?
options: Energy must be supplied to pull the bonded atoms apart
Energy is released as the atoms separate
Bonds break without any energy change
The atoms gain kinetic energy from the surroundings automatically
questions.explain: Energy has to be taken in from the surroundings to overcome the attraction holding bonded atoms together.

questions.q: Under what condition is a reaction overall exothermic in terms of bond energies?
options: The energy released making bonds is greater than the energy absorbed breaking bonds
The energy absorbed breaking bonds is greater than the energy released making bonds
No bonds are broken during the reaction
The energy absorbed and released are exactly equal
questions.explain: When more energy is released forming bonds than is taken in breaking them, there is a net release of energy, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: On a reaction pathway diagram for an endothermic reaction, where are the products drawn relative to the reactants?
options: At the same level as the reactants
questions.explain: Endothermic reactions take in energy, so the products are drawn at a higher energy level than the reactants.

questions.q: On a reaction pathway diagram, the activation energy is represented by which energy difference?
options: From the reactants up to the top of the energy barrier
From the reactants down to the products
From the products up to the top of the barrier only
The total height of the whole diagram from the axis
questions.explain: Activation energy is the energy needed to reach the peak of the barrier, measured from the reactants to the top.

questions.q: A reaction has an enthalpy change of ΔH = −92 kJ/mol. What does this tell you?
options: The reaction is exothermic and releases energy
The reaction is endothermic and takes in energy
The reaction absorbs 92 kJ of energy per mole
No energy is transferred in the reaction
questions.explain: A negative ΔH shows energy is released to the surroundings, so the reaction is exothermic.

questions.q: For H2 + Cl2 → 2HCl the bond energies are H–H = 436, Cl–Cl = 242 and H–Cl = 431 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?
questions.explain: Bonds broken = 436 + 242 = 678 and bonds made = 2 × 431 = 862, so ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ/mol.

questions.q: In a reaction the total energy absorbed breaking bonds is 1600 kJ and the total energy released making bonds is 1500 kJ. What is ΔH and what type of reaction is it?
questions.explain: ΔH = energy in − energy out = 1600 − 1500 = +100 kJ; a positive value means the reaction is endothermic.

questions.q: A student dissolves a salt in water and the temperature falls from 22 °C to 15 °C. What can be concluded?
questions.explain: The temperature of the surroundings decreased, showing thermal energy was taken in, so the process is endothermic.

questions.q: In a reaction the energy absorbed breaking bonds is 800 kJ and the energy released making bonds is 1000 kJ. What is ΔH?
questions.explain: ΔH = 800 − 1000 = −200 kJ, a negative value showing the reaction is exothermic.

specSource: Cambridge IGCSE Chemistry (0620) syllabus; Chemical Energetics
